text:
The next inquiry I would warrant is not a further certification or rejection of the criticism of J. It is a question about J′’s own successor commitment.

The relevant original occurrence is the actual revise occurrence J′, specifically its sentence: “The exact object, if one is claimed, is the set of availability values induced by selections from the per-booking alternatives together with any cross-booking compatibility relation.” The uncertainty is whether that “exact object” is licensed by the parent P9 occurrence — `6742a2a12b2f6e87cdfa889eed495f44a504365c1db35ef1e7d3fa6068e2cac4` — or whether J′ has introduced a new possibility-semantics commitment.

P9 says both things that pull in different directions. It says one can compute a lower bound and an upper bound, and that “That gives an interval, but intervals lose correlations.” It also says that when different bookings have unresolved alternatives, “availability is not a number but a set or an interval, and possibly not even a convex one.” The first sentence treats the min/max interval as a bound. The second can be read as treating availability as an exact set of possible values. P9 does not explicitly distinguish the min/max interval from the exact set of possible availabilities. J′ does distinguish them, and then assigns the exact object to selections from per-booking alternatives plus a compatibility relation. Whether that assignment is an interpretation of P9 or a new construction is unresolved.

So the successor inquiry is: Does P9 license J′’s exact-object reading — that global availability is, or ought to be represented as, the set of availability values induced by selections from per-booking alternatives, possibly restricted by a cross-booking compatibility relation — or does P9 only establish that any single number or interval must not be claimed exhaustive, leaving the exact object unspecified or outside what the snapshot supplies?

Different outcomes would change the proposed use in different ways. If P9 licenses the exact-object reading, then J′’s remedy is a legitimate refinement. The classification of P9’s objection as a criticism of an aggregation rule and a sufficiency assumption can stand, with the added distinction that exactness requires a joint-selection or possible-worlds representation, not merely an interval. If P9 does not license that reading, then J′’s remedy overcommits. The surviving point is weaker: the independent min/max interval is at most a bound, and P9’s objection blocks any claim that the interval is exhaustive; but P9 does not supply or require the exact object. The target may then be the demand for a single global availability number, or the snapshot’s sufficiency, rather than a missing compatibility relation. In that case J′’s phrase “the exact object, if one is claimed” should be rewritten as “if an exact object is claimed, P9 does not supply one,” not as a proposed representation.

Several existing claims and uses should remain distinguishable. J’s original “only under” claim is not the same as J′’s separation between a compatibility gap and a non-convexity or discreteness gap. A bound and an exact availability object are different objects. P9’s cross-booking incompatibility remains a conditional possibility, not an observation. Questioning a rule remains different from questioning a record, and accepting or rejecting a rule remains independent of accepting or rejecting data. Local alternatives, global aggregation, bounds, and correlation objections have different roles. Negative availability and whether capacity is a hard constraint remain unresolved. The E009 criticism’s proposed repairs remain proposals, not installed facts or evidence about the warehouse.

This inquiry does not need to certify that the criticism of J bore on J before asking whether J′’s way of locating that bearing is itself warranted. A negative outcome would not show that P9 has no critical force; it would relocate the target. A positive outcome would not install J′ as a repair; it would make the exact-object reading a candidate interpretation only.
